content_items.title: The Planetary Knowledge Base: an infinite solutions engine converting data into action for nature

programme.title: The Planetary Knowledge Base: an infinite solutions engine converting data into action for nature
programme.session: SYM47A Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. Part A: AI- enabled knowledge creation and extraction
programme.abstract:
The accelerating nature crisis demands more than fragmented evidence and retrospective reporting. It requires trusted systems that can turn biodiversity knowledge into action. The Planetary Knowledge Base (PKB), led by the Natural History Museum, is being developed as an AI-enabled global infrastructure to meet that need. Its success will depend on wider community participation, bringing together collections institutions, researchers, source communities, data infrastructures and users to ensure biodiversity evidence is connected, governed and applied in reciprocal ways. The PKB combines a biodiversity foundation model, trained across literature, specimen records, observations, images and genetic and environmental data, with a provenance-aware knowledge graph linking species, specimens, traits, interactions and change.

This emerging neuro-symbolic architecture is designed to extract information at planetary scale while grounding every inference in traceable evidence. Through retrieval-augmented generation, APIs and natural-language interfaces, the PKB aims to make biodiversity knowledge accessible to researchers, policymakers, communities and businesses, while reducing hallucination and opaque AI decision-making.

The PKB is conceived as an infinite solutions engine. This living infrastructure that can absorb data, test hypotheses, identify relationships and support scenario exploration for nature-positive decisions. Coupled with ecological modelling, it is intended to move from evidence synthesis to intervention design, evaluating restoration, migration and resilience planning. By linking centuries of natural history evidence with AI, digitisation and global data networks, the PKB seeks to transform collections into actionable intelligence for planetary stewardship.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by the chair as 'Vince Smith'. Content matches the programmed talk, though it covers the PKB's component projects and design principles rather than the foundation-model and neuro-symbolic details in the abstract.

content_items.summary: Vince Smith set out the Natural History Museum's vision of a Planetary Knowledge Base (PKB): infrastructure that combines knowledge graphs, foundation models and LLMs to connect fragmented biodiversity data at scale. He described phase-one projects: a new BHL discovery layer built on re-OCRed literature with Mistral, SCRIBE for label and card transcription, and an internal 'Museum Digital Backbone' built on Amazon Quick. He also described design principles that track provenance, attribution and benefit through the value chain, including remuneration models. Questions covered alignment with the CARE principles and dependence on AWS.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: The NHM is building the Planetary Knowledge Base in phases, with provenance, attribution and benefit-sharing designed in, to move biodiversity data to evidence to action at scale.
content_items.why_it_matters: It is an ambitious attempt to build community-scale AI infrastructure for biodiversity. It says openly that big tech partners and commercial revenue will be needed, and that fair returns to data contributors are an open research problem.
key_points: The big questions: moving data to evidence to action at scale, with continually growing data (10,000-20,000 records a day), unpredictable and urgent questions, provenance, and financial as well as ethical sustainability.
The PKB aligns big data infrastructures (people, observations, collections, institutions, genetics, literature) using knowledge graphs plus foundation models and LLMs, and builds services on top.
Because of the scale, the work is split into phased projects; the PKB is still in phase one.
Literature layer: BHL has been almost entirely re-OCRed with Mistral, and institutions, taxa, specimens and articles are extracted into a new discovery layer.
SCRIBE is the solution for transcribing card indexes, labels and herbarium sheets.
Museum Digital Backbone: a miniature knowledge graph plus LLM over internal, non-shareable data (grant proposals, publications), built quickly with Amazon Quick.
Design principles: preserve identifiers, provenance and licences at every step; make contributions visible through attribution; share benefits, possibly through remuneration models.
Use cases include biodiversity-change metrics sold commercially (e.g. the Biodiversity Intactness Index with Bloomberg) and work with pharma.
questions: Can large-scale data mobilisation be reconciled with the CARE principles, especially authority to control?
Is dependence on a proprietary cloud provider a risk for community infrastructure?

notable_claims.claim: The last three years have seen more innovation in this space than perhaps the previous ten, because AI is transforming the landscape.
Almost the entirety of BHL has been re-OCRed with Mistral, and entities are being extracted to form the PKB's literature layer.
The NHM sells Biodiversity Intactness Index data through Bloomberg and wants the PKB to speed up production of such metrics.
The community has to work with big tech to handle the scale, but ethically and 'eyes wide open'.

recommendations: Work with big tech partners, approaching them ethically and carefully.
future_work: Future phases of the PKB beyond phase one
Remuneration and benefit-return models for contributing communities
examples_case_studies: BHL discovery layer
SCRIBE label transcription
Museum Digital Backbone
Biodiversity Intactness Index with Bloomberg

q_and_a.question: Can this kind of massive data mobilisation be reconciled with the CARE principles?
q_and_a.answer_summary: A cautious yes. Authority to control is the hardest part. Proportional attribution could return tangible benefit to Indigenous communities, but whether it can be done is an open research question about fair AI.

q_and_a.question: There is a big AWS-shaped box in the architecture. Is the fear of proprietary enclosure warranted?
q_and_a.answer_summary: No. The community must work with some big-tech provider at this scale; AWS has given financial and technical support, and the relationship must be approached ethically, eyes wide open.

And then how do we return that value to the communities that have actually proportionately contributed to it?

content_items.title: SCRIBE: Structured Collection Record Interpretation and Bio-entity Extraction

programme.title: SCRIBE: Structured Collection Record Interpretation and Bio-entity Extraction
programme.session: SYM47A Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. Part A: AI- enabled knowledge creation and extraction
programme.abstract: There are over 120 million objects housed in natural history collections in the UK. With DiSSCo UK, 90+ institutions will be coming together, in order to make over 50% of UK natural history collections digitally available and accessible. As well as specimen imaging, a crucial goal is the building of datasets extracted from the millions of textual records. These records can include labels and index cards associated with specimens, collection registers and more. Our aim is to provide a service to aid the automatic extraction of structured data from collection records. SCRIBE (Structured Collection Record Interpretation and Bio-entity Extraction) is a new platform, being developed by a team at the NHM UK for automatic data extraction. The proposed software has the potential to revolutionise data extraction, for curation, as well as ecological analysis, by utilising Artificial Intelligence (AI), and providing an easy-to-use interface, to help unlock a plethora of data. While traditionally this task would involve manual transcription, or traditional OCR methods, taking up days and weeks, the proposed tool will for some collections, reduce this to minutes. The tool follows a computer vision and LLM based workflow that utilises customised prompts depending on visual differences within images uploaded by users, enabling users to upload datasets from varied collections concurrently. SCRIBE is a DCMS (UK Department for Culture, Media, Sport) funded and externally-funded program that will sit within the DiSSCo UK workflows. The software will be shared with institutions and evaluations will be jointly collected to further improve the online tool. Finally, the SCRIBE online tool will be supported in-house, helping to scale AI-assisted digitisation across museum and heritage sectors.

actual.identification_notes: Chair's name is ASR 'Ariana Saleily-James'. Content matches the abstract. No questions were taken because the speaker had to leave; questions were redirected to the Whova app.

content_items.summary: Arianna Salili-James reviewed the NHM's earlier data-extraction projects: ALICE label imaging, video label tracking, egg-card structuring with Google Vision (over 90% accuracy), and LLM extraction from registers, bird-skin labels, herbarium sheets and double-sided cards. Each needed its own workflow and prompts. SCRIBE, funded by DCMS and a private donor, is meant to replace these with one platform where users upload images and get structured output. It clusters mixed datasets, samples each cluster to build customised prompts, runs LLM extraction and cleans the output towards Darwin Core. The project started recently (data scientist hired in August) and runs to March 2028.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: SCRIBE aims to replace many collection-specific extraction workflows with one LLM and computer-vision platform that turns any uploaded record images into structured data.
content_items.why_it_matters: A generic, hosted extraction service could let DiSSCo UK institutions without in-house AI capacity turn labels, cards and registers into structured data, and the output would feed the Planetary Knowledge Base.
key_points: Previous NHM extraction projects each had separate workflows, training and prompts, which was inefficient.
SCRIBE targets information that can be output in a structured form (e.g. locality, habitat), not free-text transcription of books.
Users say whether an upload is homogeneous or mixed. Mixed datasets are clustered (tests with DBSCAN and PCA) before prompts are built.
Samples from each cluster go through a quick LLM entity check to customise a base prompt, then extraction runs on the full dataset, followed by cleaning and Darwin Core formatting.
Pre-processing includes auto-rotation and auto-cropping.
DiSSCo UK partners will get free token allowances; others can add their own API key. Shared outputs may feed the PKB.
Tests found handwritten and printed/typed text did equally well with LLM extraction.
Training data span vertebrates, invertebrates and botany from NHM and other UK institutions. Fungi are missing; English first, then Welsh.

content_items.title: From Historical Oology Cards to Structured Biodiversity Data: Multimodal LLM Transcription, Uncertainty Metrics, and Human Review

programme.title: From Historical Oology Cards to Structured Biodiversity Data: Multimodal LLM Transcription, Uncertainty Metrics, and Human Review
programme.session: SYM47A Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. Part A: AI- enabled knowledge creation and extraction
programme.abstract:
Historical biodiversity collections contain vast quantities of ecological information embedded in handwritten and typed archival records that remain difficult to access at scale. This project explored the use of multimodal large language models (LLMs) to transcribe and structure oological information found in historical specimen cards from the Cornell University Museum of Vertebrates. These cards record collectors' data associated with bird egg sets, breeding phenology, nest materials, and habitat descriptions collected between the late 19th and mid-20th centuries.

Using GPT-4o and Clause Sonnet 4.6-based workflows, I evaluated methods for extracting both literal transcriptions and semantically structured biodiversity data from heterogeneous card layouts containing handwriting, typewriting, annotations, and mixed narrative content. Beyond transcription accuracy, my project investigates methods for estimating review effort and transcription reliability using token-level uncertainty signals and a human-in-the-loop validation workflow. I developed a "hesitation" score based on token-level probabilities and found that this score correlates with human correction effort and may support scalable triage of records requiring expert review.

This project demonstrates how historical narrative records can become machine-actionable biodiversity data while preserving provenance, interpretability, and curatorial oversight. I discuss implications for biodiversity data mobilization and the integration of semantically enriched collection records into standards-based biodiversity infrastructures.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker's name is ASR 'Greta Pasch'. Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Grete Pasch transcribed historical oology (egg-set) cards with GPT-4o and used token log-probabilities to build a 'hesitation' score. The score does not flag every error, but it predicts how much human review a card needs. Cards were sorted into light, standard and expert review lanes; the expert lane held about a fifth of the cards but took half to two-thirds of the correction time, on both the Cornell set and 2,303 Western Foundation cards. Newer models (Gemini 3.1 Pro, Opus 5) are more accurate but do not expose log-probs; where two of them agree they are right about 997 times in 1,000, but that still does not certify a transcription.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Token-level hesitation from log-probabilities does not tell you which transcriptions are wrong, but it reliably predicts where human review effort will go.
content_items.why_it_matters: Most LLM transcription work stops at accuracy. This talk offers a practical way to triage expert review and estimate curation effort for millions of archival cards, and warns that the best models no longer expose the signals needed for it.
key_points: Nest descriptions on historical egg cards record changes in nest materials (e.g. plastic in modern Baltimore oriole nests), but they are rarely transcribed.
GPT-4o transcribed 193 of 262 cards exactly (about three in four). Typed cards were nearly perfect; handwritten cards were about two in three exact.
With logprobs enabled, the model reports its confidence in each token and its top alternatives. On a gull card it wrote '7,000' at 58% where the correct '2,000' was the runner-up at 27%.
A token counts as 'hesitant' when the top choice is less than 2.7 times as likely as the runner-up; the card hesitation score is the number of hesitant tokens.
Some cards with no hesitation still had errors (confident errors), so hesitation marks uncertainty, not correctness.
Three lanes (0-1, 2-4, 5+ hesitant tokens): median correction time was under a second in the light and standard lanes and 11 seconds in the expert lane.
The pattern held on 2,303 harder handwritten cards from the Western Foundation of Vertebrate Zoology.
Gemini 3.1 Pro and Opus 5 read about nine in ten cards correctly and agree on 98.5% of words, but even agreement is not proof.
datasets: Western Foundation of Vertebrate Zoology handwritten cards (2,303)
questions: If frontier models no longer expose log-probs, what uncertainty signal can guide review?

notable_claims.claim: GPT-4o transcribed 193 of 262 cards exactly; about two in three handwritten cards were exact.
The model hesitated exactly where it went wrong on the gull card (7,000 at 58% vs 2,000 at 27%).
Median correction time was under a second in the light and standard lanes versus 11 seconds in the expert lane.
For both collections the expert lane held about a fifth of the cards but took half to two-thirds of the correction time.
When Gemini 3.1 Pro and Opus 5 agree, they are right about 997 times out of 1,000.

recommendations: Time a sample of cards to estimate total review effort and route the hardest cards to the most experienced readers.
Use GPT-4o or open-weight models run locally if log-probability signals are needed.
results_findings: Hesitation score predicts review effort even though it does not catch every error.
Expert lane: ~20% of cards, 50-67% of correction time, replicated on a second collection.
Newer models are about 90% exact on handwritten cards but do not expose log-probs.
Model agreement is ~99.7% correct, not 100%; both models modernised 'bulrushes' spelling.
limitations: Hesitation does not catch confident errors.
The best current models do not expose log-probabilities.
Asking a model to rate its own confidence was not consistent.
future_work: Continue the work, including testing open-weight models for log-prob signals.

Ring-billed gull colony card, Oregon 1939
Great-tailed grackle card, Texas 1938 ('14 feet' read as '4 feet')

q_and_a.answer_summary: Tried at the start; the model cannot do it consistently.

q_and_a.question: Are there alternatives, and do smaller models still report probabilities?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Gemini 2.x Flash still does, though it will be deprecated, and its hesitation scores match GPT-4o's. She plans to look at open-weight models.

content_items.title: Using Large Language Models to enhance biodiversity knowledge extraction: From taxonomic treatments to graph-based knowledge systems

programme.title: Using Large Language Models to enhance biodiversity knowledge extraction: From taxonomic treatments to graph-based knowledge systems
programme.session: SYM47A Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. Part A: AI- enabled knowledge creation and extraction
programme.abstract:
Taxonomic treatments contained in checklists, floras, monographs and ecological literature compile centuries of detailed documentation on the world’s biodiversity. They typically appear as structured, peer-reviewed sections within scientific publications describing the taxonomy, morphology, distribution and ecology of a taxon, representing valuable and authoritative resources on past and present biodiversity.

Although a large collection of treatments is now freely available as Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable (FAIR) digital objects, ecological information contained within these data, such as habitat notes, remains largely underutilised, leaving untapped a vital source of knowledge for ecological modelling and conservation assessment.

Here, we present a practical framework for structuring, extracting and mapping habitat information stored in taxonomic treatments using an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted, ontology-aware knowledge graph system (a formal, machine-readable representation of domain entities and their relationships). This work forms part of a broader initiative aimed at improving the mapping of data-poor species, with a focus on vascular plants.

We propose to (a) create a knowledge graph to store evidence related to plant species habitats, (b) link this graph with semantic environmental and geospatial layers, and (c) connect this system to a large language model (LLM) to automate, query and reason over this complex knowledge base.

By reducing hallucinations and linking extracted habitat information to spatial layers, we demonstrate a viable pathway towards more reliable and transparent geospatial AI applications, supporting a more responsible use of generative AI for species distribution and habitat mapping.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Yann Ondoh' and thanked as 'Ian'; he gives his affiliation as UNEP-WCMC. Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Ian Ondo presented a framework that turns habitat information in taxonomic treatments into a structured, evidence-traceable knowledge base. Plazi TreatmentBank RDF becomes a source graph; an instruction-tuned LLM (Qwen 2.5) extracts explicit habitat statements into an evidence graph; the evidence is linked to environmental ontologies, WWF/One Earth terrestrial ecoregions and IUCN habitat classes. A trained habitat-environment compatibility model (HECC) put the correct ecoregion in its top three 75% of the time (top five 87%), and 65% zero-shot. A data-deficient Dalbergia species showed that the model's most compatible ecoregions matched its few known GBIF occurrences.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Taxonomic treatments hold underused habitat knowledge that LLMs and a provenance-preserving knowledge graph can structure and link to ecoregions, helping map data-poor species.
content_items.why_it_matters: There is no comprehensive resource for species habitat preferences. Mining treatments with traceable evidence could support conservation assessments of data-deficient species.
key_points: Plazi's TreatmentBank has made over 1.2 million treatments from about 94,000 articles machine accessible, but their ecological content is not immediately reusable.
There are structured resources for taxonomy and occurrences, but nowhere comprehensive to ask what habitat a species prefers.
Framework: TreatmentBank RDF -> source graph (publication and treatment structure) -> AI habitat extraction -> evidence graph -> integration with environmental and spatial knowledge.
Existing standards and ontologies are reused wherever possible rather than new vocabularies.
Qwen 2.5 is prompted to extract only explicit habitat statements, not to infer from altitude, place names or coordinates, and to return nothing when there is none.
Around 40,000 treatment sections were processed. HECC, an embedding model, learns semantic compatibility between habitat text and ecoregion descriptions.
Ecoregion retrieval: correct in top 3 75%, top 5 87%; zero-shot ecoregions 65%.
questions: How should free-text habitat descriptions be normalised against ontologies such as ENVO?

notable_claims.claim: Over 1.2 million taxonomic treatments from about 94,000 articles are now machine accessible through TreatmentBank.
There is no comprehensive resource to answer what habitats species prefer.
The compatibility model placed the correct ecoregion in the top three 75% of the time and top five 87%, dropping to 65% for unseen ecoregions.

results_findings: Top-3 ecoregion retrieval 75%, top-5 87%, zero-shot 65%.
For a data-deficient Dalbergia with four GBIF records, the most compatible ecoregions matched observed occurrences.
limitations: Performance drops for ecoregions not seen in training.
Talk was compressed and later slides skipped.
examples_case_studies: Data-deficient Dalbergia species (ASR 'Dalbergia menoides') from Thailand and the Malay Peninsula, habitat mangrove swamps along rivers

q_and_a.question: How is natural-language habitat text mapped to ecoregion categories? Is it normalised to ENVO first?
q_and_a.answer_summary: No intermediate normalisation. He trained an embedding model on ecoregion descriptions (from One Earth) and habitat text from treatments with known ecoregions, so it learns the semantics of how each ecoregion is described rather than name matching.

content_items.title: Automated data transcription and Darwin Core field itemization from insect specimen labels using machine learning

programme.title: Automated data transcription and Darwin Core field itemization from insect specimen labels using machine learning
programme.session: SYM47A Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. Part A: AI- enabled knowledge creation and extraction
programme.abstract: A mass digitization project of pinned insects is currently undertaken at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History (NMNH). With a conveyor system, up to 1,500 specimens and all associated data labels (two to several) are digitized each day. To mobilize the primary biodiversity data from these specimens/labels, adding them to the institutional database, and sharing them through GBIF, the label data need to be transcribed and itemized into Darwin Core fields. The two currently available options are (1) manual transcription and itemization by a human or (2) automated transcription by a tool and manual data itemization by a human. Here, we present a tool, Labellum, that goes further and is developed to transcribe all written information found on labels (whether handwritten or printed) from a specimen and automatically itemize all data into Darwin Core fields. The tool has been developed and trained on a data-set of labels from prior digitization projects at the NMNH. It uses Yolo (You Only Look Once) (v8.3.222) and Llama (v4) libraries and the Gemma 3 (12B) model for transcription and itemization. Initial, promising results using these libraries were obtained in the fall of 2025, and with further improvements, especially training on Darwin Core fields and institution-specific label data, Labellum has an accuracy of >97% transcription efficacy and a similar accuracy on Darwin Core field assignment. Labellum will be made available for use on a local machine in a self-contained environment without the need for installation of specific software. The tool has been trained on insect labels, but can be utilized on labels of other organism groups. This will allow other natural history collections to utilize Labellum in transcribing and itemizing digitized labels.

content_items.summary: Torsten Dikow described Labellum, built with University of Maryland students, which transcribes pinned-insect labels from the NMNH conveyor digitisation project and itemises the text into Darwin Core fields. The three-step pipeline uses YOLO to extract labels (about 95%), a Gemini/Gemma 3 12B model to transcribe (about 82%), and Gemini to sort text into Darwin Core 'buckets' using prompts with controlled vocabularies and field definitions. On 100 labels generated from his research database, country and verbatim date were 98-99% correct and genus/epithet errors were 7-10%, but catalogue numbers (USNMENT) were often missed or misread.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Labellum goes beyond label OCR to itemise insect-label text into Darwin Core fields, with high accuracy for most fields but problems with catalogue numbers.
content_items.why_it_matters: At up to 1,500 specimens a day from a conveyor, human transcription is a bottleneck; automated Darwin Core itemisation could speed up data mobilisation to GBIF for many collections.
key_points: NMNH is digitising about 360,000 of its 2.4 million pinned pollinators (bees, beetles, butterflies, flies) since June 2025, using a Picturae conveyor at up to 1,500 specimens per day.
Current transcription is by an external vendor (Alembo) with no interpretation (e.g. 'CA' is not expanded to California).
Published tools extract label text as a long string; Labellum's goal is Darwin Core itemisation.

content_items.title: LLM-Based Pipeline for Extracting Nomenclatural Acts from Taxonomic Literature

programme.title: LLM-Based Pipeline for Extracting Nomenclatural Acts from Taxonomic Literature
programme.session: SYM47A Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. Part A: AI- enabled knowledge creation and extraction
programme.abstract: The International Plant Names Index (IPNI) is a critical global resource for plant nomenclature, supporting biodiversity research, conservation and taxonomic data [IPNI]. However, nomenclatural acts published in taxonomic journals are still largely dependent on manual extraction to populate the resource. This is a labour-intensive process requiring IPNI staff to screen publications and manually transcribe nomenclatural details into the database, creating bottlenecks that reduce the pace of biodiversity data collection. We developed an automated extraction pipeline that processes taxonomic PDFs and outputs structured nomenclatural data using Large Language Models (LLMs). The pipeline combines PDF-to-markdown conversion, section filtering and a two-pass extraction architecture. The first pass identifies relevant taxonomic treatments and nomenclatural acts. The second pass extracts comprehensive nomenclature information from each treatment using schemas. These schemas are designed to capture various key features including name components, authorship, publication details, type specimen information, geographic details, basionyms and other metadata such as distribution. The pipeline supports configurable schemas, LLMs, and extraction targets. This enables adaptation to different biodiversity informatics workflows and document types. By transforming unstructured literature data into structured database-ready formats, this project demonstrates how LLM based processes can reduce manual extraction effort and accelerate taxonomic data mobilisation. IPNI (2026). International Plant Names Index. Published on the Internet http://www.ipni.org, The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Harvard University Herbaria & Libraries and Australian National Herbarium. [Retrieved 21 May 2026].

content_items.summary: Ishaipiriyan Karunakularatnam presented a two-stage LLM pipeline to help IPNI curators extract nomenclatural acts from taxonomic PDFs. PDFs are converted to Markdown (PyMuPDF), cleaned of tables and images, and enriched with Crossref metadata. An LLM proposes treatment anchors, which are kept only if they match real document text (exact or ≥90% fuzzy match), and each treatment is then extracted separately against a 30+ field schema. On 50 treatments, anchor detection (F1 0.79) was the weakest link, while name fields were near the ceiling. The model-agnostic LangChain pipeline (tested with a Qwen 27B model via vLLM on an HPC) sits behind a Gradio interface for curator review.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A grounded, schema-constrained two-pass LLM pipeline extracts IPNI-ready nomenclatural data well once treatments are found; finding treatment boundaries is the bottleneck.
content_items.why_it_matters: IPNI feeds global backbones like GBIF, so errors propagate downstream. The pipeline shows how to add LLM extraction to high-accuracy curation while keeping curators in control.
key_points: IPNI holds over 1.4 million plant names from 18,500 publications by 55,000+ authors, curated by Kew's Plant and Fungal Names team.
Treatment text is abbreviation-heavy, partly Latin and inconsistently formatted, so rule-based parsing does not generalise; curation is manual and slow.
Pre-processing: PyMuPDF PDF-to-Markdown, removal of images, captions and tables, Crossref metadata with fallback defaults.
Anchor detection: the LLM proposes treatment starts, which are grounded against document lines by exact then fuzzy matching (90% similarity threshold) to prevent hallucinated anchors.

Each treatment is extracted separately to keep context small, against a finite schema of 30+ fields (taxonomy, basionym, types, collection, geography, optional descriptions). Failed validations are logged without stopping the paper.
Model-agnostic through LangChain (Hugging Face transformers locally or vLLM on HPC). Small 7B models hallucinated more and were unreliable on long treatments.
Preliminary evaluation on 50 treatments: anchor detection F1 0.79; name fields near the ceiling conditional on detection.
Output is not for direct ingestion; curator review is required. A Gradio UI lets curators drop PDFs and download CSV/JSON.
standards: International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants
datasets: IPNI records as ground truth (50 treatments)

An anchor only survives if it corresponds to a real span of text in the document rather than something the model has reconstructed.
Anchor detection, at an F1 score of 0.79, is the weakest link since everything downstream is conditioned on it.

Name fields near the ceiling; high precision and recall for genus and epithet conditional on detection.
Extra fields not in IPNI (e.g. etymology, regions) were also captured.
limitations: Formatting varies across journals, which mainly hurts anchor detection (treatments cited in text, notes or tables of contents).
Publication metadata skipped when not in Crossref.
Occasional hallucination in dense treatments, e.g. multi-author collector names truncated.
Requires curator validation; not for direct ingestion.

Treatment compared with the live IPNI record

q_and_a.answer_summary: Descriptions are optional for IPNI, so they were not used in tests so far, but the model can extract them at scale.

content_items.title: Extracting Structured Biodiversity Knowledge from Literature with AI-Assisted Workflows

programme.title: Extracting Structured Biodiversity Knowledge from Literature with AI-Assisted Workflows
programme.session: SYM47A Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. Part A: AI- enabled knowledge creation and extraction
programme.abstract:
While AI and large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to accelerate scientific discovery and support knowledge generation, their effectiveness strongly depends on the availability of structured, interoperable, and machine-readable data. In biodiversity and ocean sciences, however, a significant portion of valuable information remains embedded in scientific articles, reports, and grey literature, making it difficult to access, reuse, and integrate into digital infrastructures.

To address this challenge, the St Lawrence Global Observatory (SLGO) developed an AI-assisted workflow capable of extracting not only structured metadata, but also tabular datasets and sensitive information from unstructured scientific documents. OCR-based table extraction automates the conversion of tabular information embedded in scientific PDFs into structured, machine-readable datasets, including the reconstruction of fragmented multi-page tables into unified data structures. Unlike narrative text, extracted tables can be readily integrated into ETL pipelines and downstream analytical workflows, reducing manual preprocessing while improving interoperability and reuse within biodiversity and ocean data systems, such as the Ocean Biodiversity Information System (OBIS) and Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF).

In this session, we will present the extraction pipeline, from document ingestion and preprocessing to metadata generation, table extraction, validation, and packaging. We will also discuss current challenges and opportunities related to AI-assisted data extraction, including reproducibility, provenance and model bias. This work highlights AI’s potential to support FAIR principles while ensuring transparency and quality control.

actual.identification_notes: Virtual talk played as a recording. Speaker introduced as 'Yağmur Güleç', a programmer analyst at OGSL (the French acronym for SLGO). The talk covers only the table-extraction part of the abstract; metadata and sensitive-information extraction were not presented.

content_items.summary: Yağmur Güleç presented SLGO's in-house tool for extracting tables from PDFs in grey literature. It uses the text layer for born-digital pages and falls back to Tesseract OCR only for scanned pages. A demo showed PDF upload, table detection with bounding boxes, previews and export of each table to CSV, with merged cells represented as empty cells. On 19 born-digital documents, human validation gave 83% precision and 67% recall. False positives were mostly lists of tables and tables of contents; missed tables were mostly one- or two-column tables.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A hybrid text-layer/OCR tool can free tables from grey-literature PDFs into CSV with about 83% precision, but it misses a third of tables, especially narrow ones.
content_items.why_it_matters: Much St. Lawrence biodiversity data is trapped in report tables. Automating their extraction could feed ETL pipelines toward standardised datasets for OBIS and GBIF.
key_points: SLGO, founded in 2005 with 60+ partners, provides open data on the St. Lawrence ecosystem and is one of three CIOOS regional associations.
A large share of biodiversity information sits in grey literature (reports, theses, field notes) and its tables fail the FAIR principles.
The tool uses the PDF text layer for born-digital pages and Tesseract OCR only when needed, avoiding costly OCR.
Interface: upload a PDF, browse pages, list detected tables with bounding boxes, preview and export each table as CSV.
Merged cells are represented as empty cells in the reconstructed CSV.
Evaluation on 19 born-digital documents: precision 83%, recall 67% (roughly 75% overall).
False positives: lists of tables and tables of contents; misses: mainly one- and two-column tables.

notable_claims.claim: Many PDFs in SLGO's catalogue contain tabular data that is out of reach for analysis and reuse.
On 19 born-digital documents the tool achieved 83% precision and 67% recall.
The tables most often missed were one- and two-column tables.

False positives are mostly tables of contents and lists of tables.
limitations: No scanned-table test set yet.
One-third of tables missed.

Hybridise Tesseract with PaddleOCR

content_items.title: Automated Landmark Detection for Scalable Morphometric Data Extraction from Digitized Fish Collections

programme.title: Automated Landmark Detection for Scalable Morphometric Data Extraction from Digitized Fish Collections
programme.session: SYM47B Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
programme.abstract:
Morphometric analysis is fundamental to studying biological shape variation, taxonomy, and biodiversity patterns, yet large-scale research remains constrained by the time and labor required for manual landmark annotation. As natural history collections increasingly digitize specimen images, the need for scalable and AI-ready approaches to morphological data extraction is rapidly increasing.

Here, we present a machine learning workflow for automated landmark detection in two-dimensional fish specimen images, built on a standardized anatomical annotation framework derived from established morphometric research. The model was trained and evaluated on manually annotated collection images to assess landmark detection accuracy across a diverse range of specimens.

Performance was evaluated using Euclidean distances between reference and predicted landmarks. Accuracy varied across anatomical regions, with external body outline landmarks achieving the highest precision. Species-level variation in performance was also observed, suggesting that morphology and imaging conditions both influence detection accuracy. Together, these results demonstrate that machine learning can reliably automate landmark detection in digitized collection images offering a scalable pathway toward AI-ready morphometric datasets for biodiversity research and natural history collections.

actual.identification_notes: First talk of SYM47B; speaker introduced as 'Bahadır Altuntas'. He acknowledges NSF and the Imageomics project (the university name in the acknowledgements is garbled). No questions were taken because the talk ran over time.

content_items.summary: Bahadir Altintas presented a dlib-based machine-learning workflow for automatically placing 28 anatomical landmarks on images of Notropis minnows from museum collections. Fish are detected and cropped, landmarks are predicted, and predictions are compared with manual StereoMorph annotations. On 250 test images accuracy was 95% at a 0.02 error threshold and 85.3% at 0.01. Outline landmarks and the eye were most accurate; inner landmarks and curved, folded or dorsal-view specimens were hardest. Accuracy varied by species from about 66% to near 100%.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A lightweight dlib shape-regression model can automate most fish landmarking from museum images, but inner landmarks and variable specimen poses remain hard.
content_items.why_it_matters: Manual landmarking limits morphometric studies. Automated landmarks could make digitised collection images an AI-ready source for large-scale shape analyses.
key_points: Dataset: 48 Notropis species, 28 landmarks from the literature, 217 training and 250 test images.
Manual annotation with the StereoMorph R package produced coordinates for training.
dlib was chosen for being fast, lightweight, CPU-efficient and extendable from face-landmark models; it uses regression to predict landmark positions.
Pipeline: detect the fish in the museum image, crop, predict landmarks.
Accuracy by Euclidean distance: 95% at 0.02 threshold, 85.3% at 0.01.
Outline landmarks were more accurate than inner-body ones; the eye was very accurate, perhaps because of its distinctive shape.
Per-species accuracy ranged from ~100% (N. chalybaeus) to 65.97% (N. buchanani), about 34% variation.
Low-accuracy cases were curved, folded, dorsal-view or differently photographed specimens.

notable_claims.claim: Automated landmarking reached 95% accuracy at a 0.02 error threshold and 85.3% at 0.01.
Outline landmarks were more accurate than inner body landmarks.
Accuracy varied by about 34% across species.

results_findings: 95% / 85.3% accuracy at the two thresholds.
Eye landmarks most accurate; inner landmarks least.
limitations: Small training dataset; manual annotation of 28 landmarks is time-consuming.
Inner landmarks hard to predict.
Museum images vary widely in pose and quality.

Adapt pose-estimation deep learning models for landmarking
Include more varied image types

content_items.title: Contained Agentic Workflow for Literature Analysis and Data Extraction in Museum Collections

programme.title: Contained Agentic Workflow for Literature Analysis and Data Extraction in Museum Collections
programme.session: SYM47B Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
programme.abstract:
As agentic AI systems become more capable, they offer new opportunities for interacting with complex digital infrastructures, specialist literature and collections data. These systems can move beyond single-purpose language models or fixed Retrieval-Augmented Generation workflows by supporting more flexible, context-aware interactions with knowledge. However, highly versatile agentic systems also raise important concerns around cyber security, governance, compute requirements and token costs, particularly when deployed at institutional scale.

This presentation explores the use of local LLMs and agentic workflows for the analysis of scientific literature and the extraction of structured data relevant to research and museum collections. Operating on local hardware, the system is designed to ingest, interpret and curate knowledge from research papers, reports and archival documents, linking extracted information to existing collections records and domain knowledge.

Using Dell GB10 systems and high-performance devices, we demonstrate how contained LLM workflows can identify taxonomic, morphological, geographic and ecological information within text, converting narrative scientific knowledge into structured, machine-readable data. This enables the enrichment of collections databases and supports the integration of external knowledge sources into digitisation workflows.

By operating within a local/on-device environment, the approach maintains control over data processing. Live demonstrations will show how local LLMs and agentic systems can augment research and curation workflows by helping researchers and curators unlock information contained within scientific literature and integrate it directly into research and collections-based work.

actual.identification_notes: Speaker names himself; the chair thanks 'Steve'. The project is with Jack Hollister of the NHM. The live demo had screen-sharing problems. Content is narrower than the abstract: a literature-exploration RAG prototype rather than a demonstration of structured data extraction.

content_items.summary: Steen Dupont demonstrated Kvasir, a prototype built mostly by coding agents (Codex) that runs fully on local hardware. It ingests a personal literature corpus with Docling, stores it in Neo4j and Qdrant, and lets an OpenClaw agent with a local Qwen model answer questions and explore papers. The demo ingested papers into 696 chunks and showed papers broken into sections with their references plotted over time, to characterise papers and trace evidence across the corpus. He argued for local AI for security, noted that optimised local models are improving, and suggested shared edge machines (e.g. a Dell GB10 serving 10-20 users) as institutional infrastructure, with the agent as a pluggable orchestration layer.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Contained, local agentic RAG over a literature corpus is feasible on a laptop or shared edge machine, avoiding the security worries of cloud agents in museums.
content_items.why_it_matters: Museums worry about releasing agents on institutional data. This prototype shows a low-cost, offline route to experimenting with LLM literature analysis.

Motivation: better visibility of a PhD literature corpus: most-cited works, citation timing, references per section, without reading every paper.
Architecture: OpenClaw agent orchestrator, Qwen 3.6 main model, Docling parsing, Codex-written Python scripts, Neo4j graph and Qdrant vector store, Kokoro for audio.
Demo: two papers ingested, 696 chunks created, a paper view with sections, references per section and their publication years.
Idea: the distribution of references (introduction-heavy vs conclusion-heavy) characterises paper type.

A GB10-class edge machine could serve 10-20 users on ordinary laptops instead of expensive individual machines.
The agent acts as an orchestration layer, so new Docker-hosted models (e.g. vision) can be plugged in without rebuilding.

A shared edge machine could let 10 or 20 users run such workflows from normal institutional laptops.

Demo hampered by screen-sharing issues.

q_and_a.answer_summary: Yes, the agent could do it and the LLM can already output tables, but much validation is needed; the UI 'has to be one button, because if not, it doesn't work'.

content_items.title: Curation through citation: using AI and a knowledge graph to curate DNA barcodes

programme.title: Curation through citation: using AI and a knowledge graph to curate DNA barcodes
programme.session: SYM47B Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
programme.abstract:
Recent work on visualising DNA barcode data in the BOLD database withBOLD View has revealed numerous records that are problematic or incomplete. Common problems are a lack of formal identification ("dark taxa" in the original sense), a lack of geographic coordinates, and missing information on type status.

Often the quality of a barcode record can be improved by consulting the paper that published the DNA barcode sequence. Papers frequently contain details on sampling localities, and an informally named taxon may subsequently have been described. For example, the barcode LEASZ362-22, published in the dataset "Lepidoptera of Cottian Alps" https://doi.org/10.5883/DS-LEPICOTT, is identified only to genus level as "Denisia". The DS-LEPICOTT dataset is cited by Huemer et al. (2023) https://doi.org/10.3390/d15020214, which in turn is cited by Huemer (2024) https://doi.org/10.3897/alpento.8.127794, which describes the new species, Denisia cryptica, for which the barcode LEASZ362-22 is from the holotype. Following this chain of connections resolves the identity of a dark taxon.

For this kind of curation to be feasible at scale we need to be able to discover these connections automatically. One way to do this is to create databases of the intermediate connections, especially citations between papers, and citations of data. Some of these links (such as papers citing papers) are available in existing databases, others have to be assembled by text mining or record matching.

This talk describes constructing this knowledge graph, and the role of AI tools both in constructing the graph and in enabling users to query the graph using natural language. Then talk will argue that a richly connected knowledge graph has the potential to improve the quality of biodiversity databases.

actual.identification_notes: Chair names 'Roderic Page' and later thanks 'Rhodri'/'Frederick' (ASR). The speaker says the talk is largely a rehash because the new work was not ready.

content_items.summary: Roderic Page asked what concrete value knowledge graphs deliver, and proposed curation of DNA barcode data as an answer. Using his BOLD View site, he showed BOLD records with bad or missing coordinates, vague or informal names, and names hidden behind GenBank links. Some can be fixed by following links from the barcode to GenBank, the publishing paper's DOI and a holotype, which is more than internal-consistency data cleaning. The barriers are extracting specimen and sequence codes from literature (which Plazi does not do well) and linking barcodes to papers. He pointed to emerging large triple stores (Wikidata, OpenStreetMap, GBIF, BHL, Bionomia; 86 billion triples) as signs that such a graph is becoming real.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Linking barcodes, specimens and literature in a knowledge graph could fix many BOLD records, if we can reliably extract the connecting codes from papers.
content_items.why_it_matters: Barcode data train widely used identification models while many records lack species names or correct coordinates. Citation-based curation would improve data that downstream AI relies on.

BOLD View is his site for exploring barcode data and noting odd records.

Examples: a Tasmanian-endemic crustacean plotted at Australia's centroid; a record labelled only 'Caudata' that GenBank calls a snake from China; an informal name resolved via GenBank -> DOI -> paper -> holotype.
Data cleaning flags inconsistencies; fixing needs external evidence such as the literature.

He published a dataset linking ~1,500 barcode datasets to literature; GenBank links to papers are often missing.

content_items.title: Integrating Many Data Sources in iChatBio Enables Emergent Scientific Use Cases

programme.title: Integrating Many Data Sources in iChatBio Enables Emergent Scientific Use Cases
programme.session: SYM47B Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
programme.abstract: iChatBio is an AI research platform for conversational exploration and integration of open biodiversity data, developed by the Advanced Computing and Information Systems (ACIS) Laboratory at the University of Florida. iChatBio operates by pulling data from online data sources into a unifying cloud-based workspace. Data interactions are performed by a team of autonomous large language model (LLM) agents, each specialized to interact with a single data source or data type. At its initial launch in February 2025, iChatBio only included three agents to access species occurrence data from Integrated Digitized Biocollections (iDigBio), the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), and iNaturalist. To facilitate the development of new agents, we created an open source iChatBio Software Development Kit (SDK). The SDK has so far been used to develop 16 specialized agents, which have been incorporated into iChatBio to expand its scope to new data types and data sources, including Atlas of Living Australia (ALA), Biodiversity Heritage Library (BHL), Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI), GenBank, NASA Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER), Ocean Biodiversity Information System (OBIS), World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS), and supporting agents for processing data, reading PDF documents, and generating maps from georeferenced data. iChatBio's design has also seen many improvements, including better intelligence, transparency, and configurability. This presentation will demonstrate how iChatBio's integration of diverse data sources and data processing tools supports emergent scientific use cases of online data beyond what is possible within existing Web-based data portals, while avoiding transparency and reproducibility issues that are common in LLM applications.

Worked examples combined GloBI and GBIF to find predators of the white-throated dipper with records in Norway, and generated descriptions and categories for specimen images. He stressed that chat text can hallucinate but data artefacts are real and traceable, and that more agents create emergent use cases.

content_items.title: Reliable LLM-assisted curation of ecological survey data: a deployed agent bridging field collection and data curation

programme.title: Reliable LLM-assisted curation of ecological survey data: a deployed agent bridging field collection and data curation
programme.session: SYM47B Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
programme.abstract:
We describe a deployed LLM curation agent that surfaces data-quality issues beyond the reach of schema constraints across TERN's SWARM ecological-monitoring database (around 950 sites). This contribution reports the agent's design, operating envelope, and the choices we believe make LLM-assisted curation usable on research-grade biodiversity data.

The agent is a containerised Python service with a configurable backing model - Gemini Flash Lite by default - exposing seven tools: read-only SQL against SWARM, REST queries against the Paratoo Strapi API, and findings persistence. A ten-phase full scan covers coordinate validity, completeness, transect structure, lookup-table validity, ecological plausibility, orphans, soil characterisation, uniqueness, and cross-system value mismatch. A focused mode re-checks open findings only and runs daily at negligible cost. Findings persist to a curation table with severity, category, and where applicable a suggested SQL fix. The agent never writes to the database autonomously; fixes require explicit curator approval via a web dashboard.

The agent's key advantage over schema validation is ecological plausibility reasoning. Findings surfaced include growth-form heights orders of magnitude too large (decimal-place entry errors), shrubs recorded taller than the canopy, epiphytes on bare substrate, soil horizons with inverted depth ordering, visits spanning implausible durations, and near-monoculture transects at sites expected to be species-rich. These issues cannot be caught by schema constraints - they require domain knowledge about what is ecologically reasonable. We discuss the human-approval gate rationale and initial curator-led validation to characterise true-positive rate by category.

actual.identification_notes: Virtual talk played as a recording, followed by one live question. Presented on behalf of the TERN team.

content_items.summary: Andrew Tokmakoff described a deployed LLM curation agent for TERN Ecosystem Surveillance plot data. The data moved from an older system to a new EMSA-based, schema-driven app, and side-loaded data can bypass app validation. Declarative YAML rules compiled to SQL run first. The model then works through phased briefs and queries the database via a tool harness, surfacing ecologically implausible values (999 m hummock grass, shrubs taller than the canopy, inverted soil horizons). Findings go to a curator dashboard, and nothing is written without human approval. Lessons: adjudicate by class not row, never accept silence as 'no findings', and codify confirmed findings into deterministic rules.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: An LLM agent that proposes findings for curator approval, with confirmed patterns turned into deterministic rules, catches plausibility errors that schema validation misses.
content_items.why_it_matters: It is a rare deployed, cautious example of LLM-assisted curation with clear governance (no autonomous writes) and a practical recipe others can reuse.

Phased prompts ('briefs'), e.g. flag a single species across 50+ intercepts and don't reason it away by bioregion (the model once dismissed 76 intercepts as normal for arid regions).
Harness loop: brief and tools -> model requests queries -> harness runs SQL -> JSON rows back -> model reports findings -> findings table -> curator.
Every database write passes through a curator; adjudication is by class, not individual rows.
False positives (a 65 m tree in tall wet forest; 39 forest sites without point intercepts) lead to rule tuning.
Recipe: start from real problems, let the model roam, approve or reject, codify rules, use evals with known datasets.

content_items.title: Enhancing Biodiversity Georeferencing Using Large Language Models and Knowledge Graphs

programme.title: Enhancing Biodiversity Georeferencing Using Large Language Models and Knowledge Graphs
programme.session: SYM47B Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
programme.abstract:
Geographic location is one of the most important pieces of information in biodiversity occurrence records. However, many biodiversity databases document locations only as place names or textual descriptions without geographic coordinates, often introducing ambiguity due to historical names, inconsistent spellings, and overlapping administrative regions. Consequently, current georeferencing approaches either rely on gazetteer lookups, string matching, and supervised training that remain limited for low-resource biodiversity datasets where locality descriptions are sparse, ambiguous, and domain-specific.

In this study, we develop a georeferencing pipeline that combines Large Language Models (LLMs) with a knowledge graph, i.e., Wikidata, to disambiguate location names in biodiversity occurrence records. An LLM is used as a preprocessing component to normalise locality names, identify spelling errors, resolve alternate names, and determine whether a locality reference corresponds to a valid geographic entity. The cleaned locality names are then matched against Wikidata entities using the Wikidata API. Candidate entities are ranked using lexical similarity and locality context from biodiversity records. The most likely Wikidata entity is then used to retrieve and assign geographic coordinates to the record. The proposed approach is applied to herbarium data from the Manchester Museum comprising 2,442 records collected from African sites. We compared our approach with a gazetteer-only baseline using fuzzy string matching, simulating the manual process of entering a place name into a gazetteer and selecting the top-ranked result. Our study aims to improve the accuracy of biodiversity georeferencing, particularly for ambiguous and historically inconsistent locality records.

actual.identification_notes: Virtual talk played as a recording (ASR 'Roseline Gabut'/'Rosalind'). No questions from the room.

content_items.summary: Roselyn Gabud presented a georeferencing pipeline for Manchester Museum herbarium site records from Africa exported from EMu. An LLM, backed by GeoNames and Wikidata, fills missing locality hierarchy fields from narrative site descriptions, with spelling correction and per-entity fallbacks. Geographic entities are then matched from the most to the least specific level and scored by name similarity and hierarchy. A human-in-the-loop tool shows suggestions on a map, lets annotators correct them, re-run georeferencing and export back to EMu. Preprocessing cut records with only one populated locality field from 134 to 10, and records with four or more fields rose from 13 to 142.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: LLM preprocessing plus knowledge-base matching fills in locality hierarchies and proposes coordinates, with a review tool to keep humans in control.
content_items.why_it_matters: Hundreds of thousands of specimen records still await manual georeferencing; semi-automated methods that cope with sparse, ambiguous localities could clear that backlog.
key_points: Collections such as Manchester Museum and Philippine biodiversity collections hold hundreds of thousands of records still georeferenced manually.
Many records have only a continent and a narrative site name, so filtering by country or province is impossible; ambiguity comes from outdated names, spellings and overlapping names.

Preprocessing: clean and extract location text, LLM interpretation of the full description, per-entity fallback via spelling correction, GeoNames, Wikidata and LLM, then hierarchy enrichment with confidence ratings.
Georeferencing queries GeoNames, Wikidata or Wikipedia from nearest named place up to continent, scoring candidates on name similarity and hierarchy; no match leaves coordinates blank.

Knowledge bases compared on 100 records (0.1-degree threshold): GeoNames good for administrative hierarchy but limited; Wikidata broader for natural features but noisy hierarchy; Wikipedia most comprehensive but noisy and slow.
On 263 annotated records (50 train, 213 dev), completeness improved markedly after preprocessing.
datasets: Manchester Museum African collection site records

notable_claims.claim: Before preprocessing 134 site records had only one populated locality field; afterwards only 10 did.
Records with four or more populated locality fields rose from 13 to 142.

results_findings: Large gain in locality completeness after LLM preprocessing.
Each knowledge base has distinct strengths: GeoNames administrative, Wikidata natural features, Wikipedia coverage.
limitations: Suggested values can differ subtly from annotator choices (e.g. Western Cape vs City of Cape Town).

Western Cape vs City of Cape Town discrepancy

content_items.title: Validating LLM-Extracted Biodiversity Data to Preserve Scientific Meaning

programme.title: Validating LLM-Extracted Biodiversity Data to Preserve Scientific Meaning
programme.session: SYM47B Large Language Models for Biodiversity Data Discovery, Integration, and Curation. AI applications, integration, and validation
programme.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools now enable large-scale extraction of biodiversity data from published literature, offering transformative potential for repositories seeking to expand data mobilization. However, current approaches largely treat extraction as a technical problem, leaving a critical gap in preserving scientific meaning, ensuring that interpretations are reviewed and traceable, and enabling reliable reuse. As a result, biodiversity datasets may appear FAIR while subtly diverging from the scientific intent of their original sources. Here, we describe a curation and validation infrastructure for AI-assisted biodiversity data, drawing on implementation within the specialized data repository, MorphoBank. In this context, scientific meaning is preserved when extracted character and character state definitions accurately reflect the original author’s intended distinctions, without altering those distinctions. We focus on the human validation required to achieve this: AI-generated draft data are reviewed through checklist-based verification to confirm that extracted data match the source, preserve meaning, and remain linked to their evidentiary context. Through case examples from this workflow, we show how human review identifies meaning-altering errors that are not detectable through automated validation alone. Together, these validation mechanisms enable scalable data extraction while preserving the scientific meaning of the original data. We present this as a generalizable model for biodiversity data systems that rely on AI-assisted extraction from literature. Automation accelerates data drafting, but reliable reuse depends on human validation.

actual.identification_notes: Virtual talk played as a recording; chair thanks 'Guru' (ASR). Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Brooke Long-Fox explained how MorphoBank used an LLM tool, developed with intern Shreya Jariwala over about a year, to restore missing character and character-state definitions to ~600 NSF-funded phylogenetic matrices from PBDB. The tool is now a beta feature for users. It cut per-matrix curation from hours to minutes. Across 400+ papers and ~35,000 character-state entries accuracy was about 90%, but almost every matrix had some error: omissions, misaligned states, fabricated runs of characters, and specialist anatomical terms replaced with common words. Her message was that AI produces a draft and human validation keeps the data scientifically meaningful.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: LLM extraction speeds up morphological matrix curation enormously, but errors, including fabrications, appear in almost every output, so expert validation is essential.
content_items.why_it_matters: Data can look FAIR while silently changing an author's scientific meaning. Error types from real curation show why repositories must build in human validation.
key_points: MorphoBank holds 1,500+ phylogenetic morphological character matrices from thousands of published papers.
Matrices are taxa x characters scored 0/1/2 etc.; the meaning lives in character and state definitions.
NSF funding supported adding ~600 PBDB Nexus files; many lacked state definitions, which took 1-2 to 10+ hours per matrix to add by hand.
The AI tool was trained on 20-50 hand-curated datasets; it needed page hints and expected character counts to find the right tables.
Now a beta feature in MorphoBank, with a warning that AI-extracted characters may contain errors (preprint on bioRxiv).
Results: 400+ papers, ~35,000 character-state entries, ~90% estimated accuracy; about three hours of work reduced to three minutes.
Error types: omissions, dense/irregular tables, heading misalignments, fabricated states, ambiguous anatomical terms resolved wrongly.

notable_claims.claim: Errors were found in almost every AI-extracted matrix.
Over 400 papers were processed, about 35,000 character-state entries, with an estimated 90% accuracy.
The LLM sometimes fabricated runs of characters that were not in the source.

recommendations: Treat AI output as a rough draft that requires human validation before publication.
Authors should check AI-extracted characters carefully.
results_findings: ~90% accuracy over ~35,000 entries.
Curation time cut from ~3 hours to ~3 minutes per dataset, plus validation.
limitations: Old or scanned PDFs are hard to read.
Tables are difficult for the LLM.
Needs more training data to approach perfect matrices.
future_work: Continue improving the AI model and training data
examples_case_studies: Ammonoid siphuncle and external lobe characters with missing states 0 and 1

notable_moments.description: Errors in almost every extraction.

content_items.title: TDWG 2026 Unconference: pitches, topic voting and breakout report-backs

programme.title: UNC - TDWG 2026 Unconference
programme.abstract:
The Unconference is a participant-driven session designed to explore ideas inspired by the main TDWG 2026 Conference event and this year’s theme “Research and Robot-ready Biodiversity Data Standards”. Attendees can propose topics, join breakout discussions, and collaboratively examine issues of shared interest. The format provides an opportunity for all participants, in person or online, to connect with both existing and new colleagues, explore subjects in greater depth or propose new areas that haven’t been mentioned yet throughout the conference - sowing the seeds for new collaborations.

We invite participants to share their ideas on a topic board during the conference week, where others can also express their interest in the topic. With a little guidance from the organizers at the start of the session, we will work together to select and finalize discussion group topics and self-organize into breakout groups to learn, find synergy and gain new insights.

The session will end with breakout group leaders reporting insights or discussion summaries back to the whole group (e.g., what each group discovered, something learned). Participants are encouraged to carry discussions forward beyond the session though short writeups or position statements to invite broader engagement and continue collaboration.
